subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Transverse and longitudinal waves, and how the medium moves
Using wavelength, frequency, period and wave speed together
What a sound wave is
Mechanical waves compared with electromagnetic waves
Describing waves in two and three dimensions with wavefronts and rays
What happens at a boundary: reflection, refraction and transmission
Diffraction around an obstacle and through a gap
Critical angle and total internal reflection
Snell's law and refractive index
Why two-source interference needs coherent sources
Where constructive interference occurs: path difference nλ
Where destructive interference occurs: path difference (n + ½)λ
Young's double slit: the fringe spacing s = λD/d
Nodes, antinodes, amplitude and phase along a standing wave
Standing-wave patterns in strings and pipes, and their harmonics
Natural frequency, driving frequency and resonance
How damping changes the resonance curve
What the Doppler effect is, for sound and for electromagnetic waves
Wavefront diagrams for a moving source or a moving observer
What shifted spectral lines reveal about stars and galaxies

questions.q: A longitudinal wave travels in the +x direction along a slinky spring. Displacements of the coils in the +x direction are positive. At one instant, the graph of displacement s against equilibrium position x is a sine curve: s = 0 at x = 0, s = +3.0 mm at x = 10 cm, s = 0 at x = 20 cm, s = −3.0 mm at x = 30 cm and s = 0 at x = 40 cm. Where, between x = 0 and x = 40 cm, is the centre of a compression?
options: At x = 10 cm, where the displacement is greatest and positive
At x = 10 cm and x = 30 cm, where s has its greatest magnitude
At x = 20 cm, where coils on both sides are displaced towards it
At x = 0, 20 cm and 40 cm, where the displacement s is zero
optionWhy: A student who matches compressions to the crests of the graph picks this, a habit taken from diagrams that align compressions with the crests of a pressure curve. At x = 10 cm the coils on both sides are displaced forwards by nearly the same amount, so their spacing is almost normal.

A student who thinks the spring is most squashed where coils have moved furthest picks this. Compression depends on neighbouring coils being displaced by different amounts, towards each other. At x = 10 cm and 30 cm neighbouring coils have almost the same displacement, so the spacing is nearly normal.

Coils just before x = 20 cm have positive displacement (moved forwards, towards 20 cm) and coils just after have negative displacement (moved backwards, also towards 20 cm). The coils crowd together there: a compression. At x = 0 and x = 40 cm the neighbours are displaced away from the point, so those are rarefactions.

A student who applies 'compressions are at zero displacement' to every zero point picks this. Zero points alternate between compressions and rarefactions. At x = 0 and 40 cm the coils on either side are displaced away from the point, making rarefactions; adjacent compressions are one wavelength (40 cm) apart.
questions.explain: Coils just before x = 20 cm have positive displacement (moved forwards, towards 20 cm) and coils just after have negative displacement (moved backwards, also towards 20 cm). The coils crowd together there: a compression. At x = 0 and x = 40 cm the neighbours are displaced away from the point, so those are rarefactions.
questions.working: Wavelength = 40 cm (s = 0 → +max → 0 → −max → 0 between x = 0 and 40 cm). Just below x = 20 cm, s > 0: coils displaced in +x, towards 20 cm. Just above x = 20 cm, s < 0: coils displaced in −x, also towards 20 cm. So the coils crowd together at x = 20 cm (compression). At x = 0 and x = 40 cm the neighbours are displaced away from the point (rarefactions). At x = 10 cm and 30 cm neighbouring coils have almost equal displacements, so the spacing there is almost normal.

questions.q: A student measures the wavelength λ of waves on one stretched string at three frequencies f of the vibrator, keeping the tension constant: f = 20 Hz, λ = 1.50 m; f = 40 Hz, λ = 0.75 m; f = 60 Hz, λ = 0.50 m. Which conclusion do the data support?
options: The speed rises with frequency, because v = fλ and f was increased each time.
The speed is the same at each frequency, so it does not depend on the frequency.
The speed falls as the frequency rises, because the period rises as frequency does.
No conclusion is possible, as the amplitude, which sets the speed, was not measured.
optionWhy: A student who reads v = fλ as v ∝ f picks this without calculating fλ. The wavelength fell in exact proportion as f rose, so the product fλ, the speed, stayed at 30 m s⁻¹.
fλ = 20 × 1.50 = 40 × 0.75 = 60 × 0.50 = 30 m s⁻¹ in every case. The string sets the speed; raising the frequency shortens the wavelength in inverse proportion.

A student who treats period and frequency as increasing together picks this and uses v = λ/T with a growing T. In fact T = 1/f falls as f rises: T = 0.050 s, 0.025 s, 0.017 s, and λ/T = 30 m s⁻¹ each time.

A student who thinks amplitude affects wave speed picks this. The speed of a wave on a string depends on the string and its tension, not on the amplitude, and the data already show fλ constant at 30 m s⁻¹.
questions.explain: fλ = 20 × 1.50 = 40 × 0.75 = 60 × 0.50 = 30 m s⁻¹ in every case. The string sets the speed; raising the frequency shortens the wavelength in inverse proportion.
questions.working: v = fλ: 20 Hz × 1.50 m = 30 m s⁻¹; 40 Hz × 0.75 m = 30 m s⁻¹; 60 Hz × 0.50 m = 30 m s⁻¹. The speed is constant; λ is inversely proportional to f.

questions.q: The graph shows the displacement s of the air particles against position x at one instant as a sound wave travels through air along the x direction. Displacements in the +x direction are positive. Four positions P, Q, R and S are marked on the graph. Which position is at the centre of a rarefaction?
options: Point P
Point Q
Point S
Point R
optionWhy: Q and S are not both compressions, so the rarefaction is not forced onto a crest. P is a crest: the particles there are displaced furthest in +x, but their neighbours on either side are displaced by almost the same amount, so the spacing at P is normal. Where s falls through zero (Q) neighbours have moved together; where it rises through zero (S) they have moved apart. The rarefaction is at S.

Q is the other kind of zero crossing. Just to the left of Q the displacement is positive, so those particles have moved in +x, towards Q; just to the right it is negative, so those particles have moved in -x, also towards Q. Neighbours have moved together, so Q is the centre of a compression, the opposite of what is asked. Where s rises through zero (S) the neighbours have moved apart.

Correct. Just to the left of S the displacement is negative (those particles have moved in −x, away from S) and just to the right it is positive (those particles have moved in +x, also away from S). Neighbouring particles have moved apart, so S is the centre of a rarefaction. Compressions and rarefactions sit at the zero crossings of a displacement–position graph, not at its crests and troughs.

R is the trough of the graph, but a trough on the displacement graph of a longitudinal wave is not a rarefaction. The particles at R are simply displaced furthest in −x, and their neighbours on either side are displaced by nearly the same amount, so the spacing there is normal. The rarefaction is at the zero crossing where s rises through zero, S.
questions.explain: Correct. Just to the left of S the displacement is negative (those particles have moved in −x, away from S) and just to the right it is positive (those particles have moved in +x, also away from S). Neighbouring particles have moved apart, so S is the centre of a rarefaction. Compressions and rarefactions sit at the zero crossings of a displacement–position graph, not at its crests and troughs.

figure.alt: Displacement–position graph for a sound wave: displacement s of the air particles (vertical axis, positive for displacement in the +x direction) against position x. The curve is a sine wave over one and a half wavelengths starting at s = 0 at x = 0. Four positions are marked with red dots: P at the first crest (maximum positive s), Q at the next zero crossing where s falls from positive to negative, R at the trough (maximum negative s), and S at the following zero crossing where s rises from negative to positive. The origin is marked 0.

questions.q: A small loudspeaker emitting a steady note and a lamp are sealed inside a glass jar. Outside the jar a microphone and a light sensor face them. At t = 0 a pump starts removing the air from the jar. The graph shows the output of each sensor against time. Which conclusion do the two traces support?
options: The sound wave needs a material medium to reach the microphone, but the light wave does not.
The pump drew the sound out of the jar along with the air that was carrying it.
Both waves need air, but the light needed only the trace of air the pump left behind.
Only longitudinal waves need a medium; the light passed because it is a transverse wave.
optionWhy: Correct. As the air is removed the microphone output falls to zero while the light sensor output stays constant. Sound is a mechanical wave, carried by oscillations of the air particles, so with no air there is nothing to carry it. Light is an electromagnetic wave and needs no medium, so removing the air leaves it unchanged.

Sound is not a substance mixed into the air that a pump can extract: it is an oscillation of the air particles about fixed positions, and the air itself does not flow from the loudspeaker to the microphone. The trace falls because there are fewer and fewer particles left to pass the oscillation on.

The light trace does not change at all while the microphone trace falls to zero; if light also needed air, its output would fall as the air pressure dropped. Light travels through a vacuum: it is an oscillating electric and magnetic field and needs no particles at all.

Light is transverse, but that is not why it passes: transverse mechanical waves, such as waves on a rope, need a medium too. The distinction the traces show is between a mechanical wave (sound) and an electromagnetic wave (light), not between longitudinal and transverse.
questions.explain: Correct. As the air is removed the microphone output falls to zero while the light sensor output stays constant. Sound is a mechanical wave, carried by oscillations of the air particles, so with no air there is nothing to carry it. Light is an electromagnetic wave and needs no medium, so removing the air leaves it unchanged.

figure.alt: Graph of sensor output (vertical axis, no scale) against time t / s (horizontal axis, marked 0, 20, 40, 60). The pump starts at t = 0. The trace labelled 'light sensor' is a horizontal straight line at a high, constant value from t = 0 to t = 60 s. The trace labelled 'microphone' starts at a moderate value at t = 0, falls steadily, is close to zero by about t = 40 s and stays at zero to t = 60 s.

questions.q: A small loudspeaker in open air emits sound of frequency 170 Hz. The speed of sound in air is 340 m s⁻¹. A student draws a wavefront–ray diagram of the sound in a horizontal plane through the speaker. Which statement about the diagram is correct?
options: Every compression and every rarefaction has a wavefront, so neighbouring ones are 1.0 m apart.
The rays show the paths along which air is carried outward from the speaker.
Adjacent wavefronts are 2.0 m apart, both close to the speaker and far from it.
There is no sound in the gaps between the rays that are drawn on the diagram.
optionWhy: A wavefront is drawn through points that are in phase, so it passes through compressions only (or rarefactions only), not both. A compression and the next rarefaction are λ/2 = 1.0 m apart, but adjacent wavefronts on the diagram are a full wavelength, 2.0 m, apart.

Sound is a wave: the air oscillates about fixed positions and is not carried away from the speaker. A ray shows the direction in which the wave's energy travels, perpendicular to the wavefronts, not a path taken by the medium.

λ = v/f = 340/170 = 2.0 m. Wavefronts join points that are in phase (successive compressions), so neighbours are one wavelength apart, and since neither v nor f changes with distance the spacing is the same everywhere. The wavefronts are circles centred on the speaker (sections of spheres in three dimensions) and the rays are radial lines perpendicular to them.

Rays are construction lines showing the direction of energy travel; any number could be drawn. The sound wave fills the whole region around the speaker, including the spaces between whichever rays the student chose to draw.
questions.explain: λ = v/f = 340/170 = 2.0 m. Wavefronts join points that are in phase (successive compressions), so neighbours are one wavelength apart, and since neither v nor f changes with distance the spacing is the same everywhere. The wavefronts are circles centred on the speaker (sections of spheres in three dimensions) and the rays are radial lines perpendicular to them.
questions.working: λ = v/f = 340 m s⁻¹ / 170 Hz = 2.0 m. Wavefronts are drawn through points in phase (successive compressions), so adjacent wavefronts are λ = 2.0 m apart, and this spacing is the same at every distance from the speaker because v and f are unchanged. The wavefronts are circles (sections of spheres) centred on the speaker; rays are radial, perpendicular to them.

questions.q: Straight water waves of frequency 5.0 Hz travel at 0.40 m s⁻¹ across the deep part of a ripple tank towards a boundary with a shallow region, in which the wave speed is 0.20 m s⁻¹. The wavefronts are parallel to the boundary. Which statement about the waves at the boundary is correct?
options: The reflected waves have a wavelength of 8.0 cm and the transmitted waves 4.0 cm.
The transmitted waves have a wavelength of 8.0 cm, the same as that of the incident waves.
The transmitted waves have a frequency of 2.5 Hz, half that of the incident waves.
No waves are reflected at the boundary; all of the wave energy passes into the shallow water.
optionWhy: The frequency, 5.0 Hz, is the same for the incident, reflected and transmitted waves. Reflected waves travel in the deep water at 0.40 m s⁻¹, so λ = 0.40/5.0 = 8.0 cm, the same as the incident waves. Transmitted waves travel at 0.20 m s⁻¹, so λ = 0.20/5.0 = 4.0 cm: the speed halves, and so does the wavelength.

At a boundary the speed and the wavelength change together, because the frequency is fixed by the source. With v = fλ and f = 5.0 Hz, halving the speed to 0.20 m s⁻¹ halves the wavelength to 4.0 cm. Only the reflected waves, which stay in the deep water, keep the 8.0 cm wavelength.

Every wavefront arriving at the boundary produces one transmitted wavefront, so the number of wavefronts per second, the frequency, is the same on both sides: 5.0 Hz. It is the wavelength, not the frequency, that halves when the speed halves.

Wherever the wave speed changes, some of the wave is reflected and some transmitted, even at normal incidence. A weak reflected wave travels back through the deep water with the incident wavelength of 8.0 cm; the transmitted wave carries the rest of the energy at 4.0 cm wavelength.
questions.explain: The frequency, 5.0 Hz, is the same for the incident, reflected and transmitted waves. Reflected waves travel in the deep water at 0.40 m s⁻¹, so λ = 0.40/5.0 = 8.0 cm, the same as the incident waves. Transmitted waves travel at 0.20 m s⁻¹, so λ = 0.20/5.0 = 4.0 cm: the speed halves, and so does the wavelength.
questions.working: Incident wavelength λ₁ = v₁/f = 0.40/5.0 = 0.080 m = 8.0 cm. The reflected wave travels back in the deep water at 0.40 m s⁻¹ with the same frequency, so its wavelength is also 8.0 cm. The transmitted wave keeps f = 5.0 Hz, so λ₂ = v₂/f = 0.20/5.0 = 0.040 m = 4.0 cm. Part of the wave is reflected and part transmitted, even at normal incidence.

questions.q: Two radio stations broadcast from the same mast: station A at 1.0 MHz, wavelength 300 m, and station B at 100 MHz, wavelength 3.0 m. A house stands in a valley behind a hill about 200 m high, with no straight-line path from the mast to the house. Which station is more likely to be received at the house, and why?
options: Station B, because its 100 MHz waves carry more energy and so pass over the hill more easily.
Both equally, because the hill is the same size for both, and it alone fixes how much a wave diffracts.
Neither, because diffraction only occurs when the wavelength is exactly equal to the size of the hill.
Station A, because its 300 m wavelength is comparable with the hill's size, so it diffracts round it.
optionWhy: How far a wave spreads into the region behind an obstacle depends on its wavelength compared with the obstacle, not on the energy it carries. Station B's short 3.0 m wavelength is much smaller than the hill, so it diffracts very little; the hill blocks it much more effectively than it blocks station A.

The size of the obstacle only matters in comparison with the wavelength. The same 200 m hill is small relative to a 300 m wavelength but enormous relative to a 3.0 m wavelength, so the two stations' signals diffract by very different amounts.

There is no requirement for an exact match. Diffraction is noticeable whenever the wavelength is comparable with or larger than the obstacle, and it becomes stronger as the wavelength increases, so the 300 m signal spreads readily into the valley.

Diffraction around a body is significant when the wavelength is comparable with, or larger than, the size of the body. Station A's 300 m waves are of the same order as the 200 m hill and spread strongly into the valley behind it; station B's 3.0 m waves are far smaller than the hill and diffract very little, so the hill casts a radio 'shadow' for them.
questions.explain: Diffraction around a body is significant when the wavelength is comparable with, or larger than, the size of the body. Station A's 300 m waves are of the same order as the 200 m hill and spread strongly into the valley behind it; station B's 3.0 m waves are far smaller than the hill and diffract very little, so the hill casts a radio 'shadow' for them.
questions.working: Diffraction around a body is significant when λ is comparable with or larger than the body. Station A: λ = 300 m, of the same order as the 200 m hill, so the waves spread strongly into the valley behind it. Station B: λ = 3.0 m, about 70 times smaller than the hill, so it diffracts very little and the hill shadows the house. Station A is the one more likely to be received.

questions.q: The diagram shows a ray of light inside a semicircular glass block of refractive index 1.50, surrounded by air of refractive index 1.00. The ray travels along a radius to the centre C of the flat face, making the angle marked with the flat face. What happens to the ray at C?
options: It refracts into the air at 22.5° to the normal.
It refracts into the air, emerging at 35.0° to the normal.
It refracts into the air, leaving at 59.4° to the normal.
It is totally internally reflected, back into the glass.
optionWhy: This has the refractive indices the wrong way round, sin θ₂ = sin 35°/1.50. Light travels faster in air than in glass, so on leaving the glass it bends away from the normal: sin θ₂ = 1.50 sin 35°, giving 59.4°.

This uses only the refractive index of the air the light enters, as if sin θ₂ = sin θ₁/n_air with n_air = 1.00. Snell's law needs both media: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ with n₁ = 1.50 for the glass, so sin θ₂ = 1.50 sin 35° and θ₂ = 59.4°.

The 55° is measured from the flat face, so the angle of incidence is 90° − 55° = 35°. The critical angle for glass to air is sin⁻¹(1.00/1.50) = 41.8°, and 35° is less than this, so the ray leaves the glass: 1.50 sin 35° = 1.00 sin θ₂ gives θ₂ = 59.4°, bending away from the normal. Some light is also partially reflected.

Taking the marked 55° as the angle of incidence makes it exceed the 41.8° critical angle. But angles of incidence are measured from the normal, so θ₁ = 90° − 55° = 35°, which is less than the critical angle, and the ray refracts out at 59.4°.
questions.explain: The 55° is measured from the flat face, so the angle of incidence is 90° − 55° = 35°. The critical angle for glass to air is sin⁻¹(1.00/1.50) = 41.8°, and 35° is less than this, so the ray leaves the glass: 1.50 sin 35° = 1.00 sin θ₂ gives θ₂ = 59.4°, bending away from the normal. Some light is also partially reflected.
questions.working: The angle marked, 55°, is between the ray and the flat face, so the angle of incidence (from the normal) is θ₁ = 90° − 55° = 35°. Critical angle for glass to air: sin c = 1.00/1.50 ⇒ c = 41.8°. Since 35° < 41.8°, the ray refracts into the air (with some partial reflection): 1.50 sin 35° = 1.00 sin θ₂ ⇒ sin θ₂ = 0.860 ⇒ θ₂ = 59.4°. The ray enters the curved face along a radius, so it is undeviated there.

questions.q: Monochromatic light has a wavelength of 450 nm in water, of refractive index 1.33. The light passes from the water into glass of refractive index 1.50. What is its wavelength in the glass?
options: 508 nm
399 nm
450 nm
300 nm
optionWhy: A student who thinks light is faster in the medium of larger refractive index uses the ratio upside down: 450 × 1.50/1.33 = 508 nm. In glass (n = 1.50) light is slower than in water (n = 1.33), so the wavelength must decrease.
The frequency is unchanged, so λ₂/λ₁ = v₂/v₁ = n₁/n₂. λ₂ = 450 nm × 1.33/1.50 = 399 nm. The glass has the larger refractive index, so the light is slower and its wavelength shorter there.
A student who thinks only the speed changes at a boundary keeps the wavelength at 450 nm. The frequency stays the same, so the wavelength falls in proportion to the speed.
A student who uses the glass's refractive index alone, as if the light came from air, calculates 450/1.50 = 300 nm. The light comes from water, so the ratio n₁/n₂ = 1.33/1.50 must be used.
questions.explain: The frequency is unchanged, so λ₂/λ₁ = v₂/v₁ = n₁/n₂. λ₂ = 450 nm × 1.33/1.50 = 399 nm. The glass has the larger refractive index, so the light is slower and its wavelength shorter there.
questions.working: f is unchanged ⇒ λ₂/λ₁ = v₂/v₁ = n₁/n₂. λ₂ = 450 nm × (1.33/1.50) = 399 nm.

questions.q: Two identical sodium lamps placed side by side illuminate a white screen. No interference fringes can be seen anywhere on the screen. Which statement explains this?
options: The phase difference between the light from the two lamps changes rapidly and randomly, so they are not coherent.
Light waves from two separate lamps cannot superpose, so they pass through each other without interfering.
The lamps have the same frequency, so they are coherent and fringes form, but they are too fine to be seen.
Stable interference fringes can be produced only with laser light, and sodium lamps do not emit laser light.
optionWhy: Each lamp emits light in short, random bursts from many atoms, so the phase difference between the two lamps' light changes randomly millions of times a second. The light does superpose, but any pattern moves so fast that the screen appears evenly lit. A stable pattern needs coherent sources, with a constant phase difference.

A student who thinks non-coherent waves do not superpose picks this. All waves superpose: at each instant the light from the lamps interferes, but the pattern changes too quickly to be seen because the phase difference is not constant.

A student who thinks equal frequency makes sources coherent picks this. Coherence also needs a constant phase difference, and the phase of each lamp's light changes randomly. No stable fringes form at all, however fine.

A student who thinks only lasers give interference picks this. Light from a single sodium lamp, passed through a single slit and then a double slit, gives clear fringes because both slits are lit by the same wavefronts. The problem here is two independent sources.
questions.explain: Each lamp emits light in short, random bursts from many atoms, so the phase difference between the two lamps' light changes randomly millions of times a second. The light does superpose, but any pattern moves so fast that the screen appears evenly lit. A stable pattern needs coherent sources, with a constant phase difference.

questions.q: The diagram shows two point sources S₁ and S₂ in a ripple tank, vibrating in phase, and a point P on the water surface. The waves have a wavelength of 2.0 cm. On which line of the interference pattern does P lie?
options: On the first minimum to one side of the central maximum line.
On the first maximum to one side of the central maximum.
On the second maximum to one side of the central maximum.
On no maximum, because P is not equidistant from S₁ and S₂.
optionWhy: This treats a path difference of one wavelength, 2.0 cm, as a phase difference of π. One wavelength is a whole cycle, 2π, so the waves arrive in phase and P is on the first maximum; the first minimum needs a path difference of λ/2 = 1.0 cm.

S₂P = √(15.0² + 8.0²) = 17.0 cm, so the path difference is 17.0 − 15.0 = 2.0 cm = λ. For in-phase sources a path difference of nλ gives a maximum; n = 1 is the first maximum beside the central (n = 0) line.
This counts the 2.0 cm path difference as two half-wavelengths and calls it the second maximum. Maxima need a whole number of wavelengths: 2.0 cm is 1 × λ, so P is on the first maximum.

Equal distances give only the central maximum. Any path difference that is a whole number of wavelengths also gives a maximum, and here 17.0 − 15.0 = 2.0 cm = λ, so P is on the first maximum to one side.
questions.explain: S₂P = √(15.0² + 8.0²) = 17.0 cm, so the path difference is 17.0 − 15.0 = 2.0 cm = λ. For in-phase sources a path difference of nλ gives a maximum; n = 1 is the first maximum beside the central (n = 0) line.
questions.working: S₁P = 15.0 cm and S₁S₂ = 8.0 cm meet at a right angle at S₁, so S₂P = √(15.0² + 8.0²) = √289 = 17.0 cm. Path difference = 17.0 − 15.0 = 2.0 cm = 1 × λ, a whole number of wavelengths, so the waves arrive in phase: constructive interference (n = 1).

questions.q: Two loudspeakers connected to the same signal generator emit sound in phase at a frequency of 680 Hz. The speed of sound in air is 340 m s⁻¹. What is the smallest path difference that gives destructive interference?
optionWhy: A student who equates a path difference of λ with a phase difference of π (half a cycle) gives λ = 0.50 m. A path difference of λ is a phase difference of 2π, a whole cycle, so the waves arrive in phase and interfere constructively. Antiphase needs a path difference of λ/2 = 0.25 m.
A student who rearranges the wave equation as λ = f/v gets 680/340 = 2.0 and halves it to give 1.00 m. The wavelength is λ = v/f = 0.50 m, so half a wavelength is 0.25 m.
λ = v/f = 340/680 = 0.50 m. Destructive interference needs path difference = (n + ½)λ, and the smallest value is for n = 0: ½ × 0.50 m = 0.25 m.
A student who starts n at 1 uses (1 + ½)λ = 1.5 × 0.50 = 0.75 m. That path difference does give a minimum, but not the smallest one: n = 0 gives 0.25 m.
questions.explain: λ = v/f = 340/680 = 0.50 m. Destructive interference needs path difference = (n + ½)λ, and the smallest value is for n = 0: ½ × 0.50 m = 0.25 m.
questions.working: λ = v/f = (340 m s⁻¹)/(680 Hz) = 0.50 m. Destructive: path difference = (n + ½)λ; smallest for n = 0 ⇒ 0.5 × 0.50 m = 0.25 m.

questions.q: The graph shows how the intensity I of the light on a screen varies with position x in a Young's double-slit experiment. The two slits are 0.40 mm apart and each is 0.020 mm wide; the screen is 2.0 m from the slits, and monochromatic light is incident normally on them. What is the wavelength of the light?
optionWhy: Adjacent maxima on the graph are 3.0 mm apart, so s = 3.0 × 10⁻³ m. Rearranging s = λD/d gives λ = sd/D = (3.0 × 10⁻³ × 0.40 × 10⁻³)/2.0 = 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ m, orange light of 600 nm.
This divides the 12 mm between the outermost maxima by the five maxima counted, giving 2.4 mm. There are only four fringe spacings between five maxima, so s = 12/4 = 3.0 mm and λ = 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ m.

This uses the slit width, 0.020 mm, in place of the slit separation. The fringe separation s = λD/d depends on the distance d between the centres of the slits, 0.40 mm, giving λ = 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ m. The slit width affects only the brightness envelope.

This substitutes s = 3.0 (millimetres) alongside d in metres and D in metres. All lengths must be in the same unit: s = 3.0 × 10⁻³ m gives λ = 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ m. A wavelength of 0.6 mm would be far into the infrared, not visible light.
questions.explain: Adjacent maxima on the graph are 3.0 mm apart, so s = 3.0 × 10⁻³ m. Rearranging s = λD/d gives λ = sd/D = (3.0 × 10⁻³ × 0.40 × 10⁻³)/2.0 = 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ m, orange light of 600 nm.
questions.working: From the graph, adjacent maxima are at x = 0, 3, 6 mm, so the fringe separation is s = 3.0 mm = 3.0 × 10⁻³ m. s = λD/d ⇒ λ = sd/D = (3.0 × 10⁻³ m × 0.40 × 10⁻³ m)/2.0 m = 6.0 × 10⁻⁷ m (600 nm).

figure.alt: Graph of intensity I (vertical axis, no scale) against position on the screen x / mm (horizontal axis, ticks labelled −6, −3, 0, 3, 6). The curve is a series of five equally tall, equally spaced smooth peaks with the intensity falling to zero between them: maxima at x = −6, −3, 0, 3 and 6 mm and minima midway between them.

questions.q: The diagram shows the envelope of a standing wave on a string of length L, driven by a vibrator at its left end and fixed at its right end. The amplitude of the vibrator is so small that both ends of the string can be treated as nodes. P and Q are points on the string. At one instant, P has its maximum displacement, upward. Which describes Q at that instant?
options: Q is displaced upward by exactly the same amount as P.
Q is moving through its equilibrium position.
Q is displaced upward but by a smaller amount than P.
Q is displaced downward by the same amount as P.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the whole string moves up and down together picks this. Points in adjacent loops are in antiphase: while the left-hand loop bulges upward the right-hand loop bulges downward, so Q is displaced downward when P is displaced upward.

A student who applies the travelling-wave rule Δφ = 2πx/λ picks this: P and Q are λ/4 apart (λ = L here), giving a phase difference of π/2, so Q would be at zero displacement when P is at its maximum. In a standing wave all points within one loop are in phase and points in adjacent loops are in antiphase, so Q is at its maximum displacement, downward, at that instant.

A student who pictures the wave weakening as it travels away from the vibrator, with the string rising and falling as one, picks this. The amplitude of a point on a standing wave depends only on its distance from the nearest node: P and Q are the same distance from the midpoint node, so their amplitudes are equal, and because they lie in adjacent loops they oscillate in antiphase, so Q is displaced downward by the same amount as P is displaced upward.

P and Q are the same distance from the node at the midpoint, so they have equal amplitudes, and they lie in adjacent loops, on opposite sides of that node, so they oscillate in antiphase. When P is at its maximum displacement upward, Q is at its maximum displacement downward, and the two displacements are equal in size.
questions.explain: P and Q are the same distance from the node at the midpoint, so they have equal amplitudes, and they lie in adjacent loops, on opposite sides of that node, so they oscillate in antiphase. When P is at its maximum displacement upward, Q is at its maximum displacement downward, and the two displacements are equal in size.

figure.alt: Diagram of a horizontal string running from a small box labelled vibrator at the left to a fixed support at the right. The standing-wave envelope has two equal loops: a solid upper curve and a dashed lower curve that meet on the dashed equilibrium line at both ends and at the midpoint of the string. A dimension line below marks the two halves of the string as L/2 and L/2. Two red dots on the equilibrium line mark points P and Q: P is a quarter of the way along the left-hand loop from the midpoint node, and Q the same distance to the right of the midpoint node in the right-hand loop.

questions.q: The diagram shows the displacement envelope of the air in a pipe of length L = 0.85 m that is closed at one end and open at the other. The speed of sound in the air is 340 m s⁻¹. What is the frequency of the sound?
options: 600 Hz
300 Hz
200 Hz
385 Hz
optionWhy: A student who takes the full loop between the two nodes as a whole wavelength (and the last quarter of the pattern as half a wavelength) gets L = 3λ/2, λ = 0.567 m and f = 600 Hz. A loop from node to node is half a wavelength, so L = 3λ/4 and f = 300 Hz.

The envelope shows a node at the closed end, an antinode a quarter-wavelength in, a node at the half-wavelength point and an antinode at the open end: the pipe holds three quarter-wavelengths, so λ = 4L/3 = 1.13 m and f = 340/1.13 = 300 Hz.

A student who counts the two nodes and calls the pattern the second harmonic, f = 2 × v/(4L), gets 200 Hz. A pipe closed at one end has only odd harmonics; with three quarter-wavelengths in the pipe this is the third harmonic, f = 3 × v/(4L) = 300 Hz.
A student who multiplies the speed by the wavelength, f = vλ = 340 × 1.13, gets 385 Hz. Frequency is speed divided by wavelength: f = v/λ = 340/1.13 = 300 Hz.
questions.explain: The envelope shows a node at the closed end, an antinode a quarter-wavelength in, a node at the half-wavelength point and an antinode at the open end: the pipe holds three quarter-wavelengths, so λ = 4L/3 = 1.13 m and f = 340/1.13 = 300 Hz.
questions.working: The closed end is a displacement node and the open end an antinode. The pattern has a node at the closed end, one more node inside the pipe and an antinode at the open end, so L = 3λ/4: λ = 4L/3 = 4 × 0.85 m / 3 = 1.13 m. f = v/λ = 340 m s⁻¹ / 1.133 m = 300 Hz (the third harmonic of the pipe).

figure.alt: Diagram of a horizontal pipe drawn as a shaded rectangle with a thick wall at the left end, labelled closed end, and no wall at the right end, labelled open end; the length between the ends is marked L = 0.85 m. Inside the pipe the displacement envelope is drawn as a solid upper curve and a dashed lower curve. They meet on the dashed centre line at the closed end and again at a point two thirds of the way along the pipe, and are furthest apart one third of the way along and at the open end, where the envelope ends wide open.

questions.q: The graph shows how the steady amplitude of a lightly damped mass–spring system depends on the frequency of the periodic force that drives it. The amplitude of the driving force is kept constant while its frequency is reduced slowly from 8.0 Hz to 2.0 Hz. Which describes the amplitude of the mass–spring system during this change?
options: It falls throughout, because a slower driving force transfers less energy to the system.
It stays the same throughout, because the amplitude of the driving force does not change.
It rises to a maximum as the driving frequency passes about 5 Hz, then falls again.
It rises to a maximum near 5 Hz then stays there, as the system now oscillates at its natural frequency.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a faster driver always gives a bigger response picks this. The amplitude depends on how close the driving frequency is to the natural frequency, not on how high it is: the graph rises as the frequency comes down towards 5 Hz and only falls once the frequency is below that.

A student who thinks the size of the response is set only by the size of the force picks this. With the same force amplitude the response varies strongly with frequency, as the graph shows: small far from 5 Hz and largest at resonance.

The graph peaks at about 5 Hz, the natural frequency of the system. As the driving frequency falls from 8.0 Hz it approaches the natural frequency and the amplitude grows, is largest when the driving frequency passes about 5 Hz (resonance), and then decreases again as the driving frequency moves further below the natural frequency towards 2.0 Hz.

A student who thinks a driven system settles at its own natural frequency picks this: once the driver has passed 5 Hz the system is imagined to keep resonating on its own. After the transient dies away a driven system oscillates at the driving frequency, whatever that is; the graph shows that when the driving frequency has fallen to 2.0 Hz the steady amplitude is small again.
questions.explain: The graph peaks at about 5 Hz, the natural frequency of the system. As the driving frequency falls from 8.0 Hz it approaches the natural frequency and the amplitude grows, is largest when the driving frequency passes about 5 Hz (resonance), and then decreases again as the driving frequency moves further below the natural frequency towards 2.0 Hz.
questions.working: The peak of the response curve, read from the graph, is at about 5 Hz: this is the natural frequency of the system. Reducing the driving frequency from 8.0 Hz brings it towards 5 Hz, so the amplitude rises; it is greatest as the driving frequency passes about 5 Hz (resonance) and then falls as the driving frequency continues down to 2.0 Hz.

figure.alt: Graph of amplitude (vertical axis, no scale) against driving frequency / Hz (horizontal axis, marked 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10). The curve starts at a small amplitude at low frequency, rises slowly at first and then steeply to a single sharp peak close to 5 Hz, then falls steeply and flattens out towards a very small amplitude by 8 Hz and beyond.

questions.q: Curve X on the graph shows how the steady amplitude of a driven oscillator varies with driving frequency. One change is then made to the apparatus, and the measurements are repeated to give curve Y. Which change was made?
options: The damping acting on the oscillator was made smaller.
The amplitude of the driving force was reduced.
The natural frequency of the oscillator was lowered.
The damping acting on the oscillator was increased.
optionWhy: A student who thinks damping makes a system stiffer, raising its resonant frequency, reads the lower peak frequency of Y as a sign of less damping. Damping lowers the peak frequency slightly, and Y's lower, broader peak confirms that the damping was increased.

A student who thinks damping cannot alter the steady amplitude of a driven system looks for another cause and blames the driver. A smaller driving force would scale the whole curve down, including the parts far from resonance, and would not shift or broaden the peak. Only Y's peak region differs from X, which is the effect of increased damping.

A student who thinks damping scales the whole response curve down rules damping out, because the curves coincide away from the peak, and attributes the small shift to a change in the natural frequency. A lower natural frequency would move the whole peak, not make it three times lower and much broader; a lower, broader peak at a slightly lower frequency is the signature of increased damping.

Curve Y has the three signs of heavier damping: a lower maximum amplitude, a wider peak, and a peak at a slightly lower frequency. Away from resonance the curves coincide, which is also expected, because damping matters most near resonance, where the amplitude is limited by the energy dissipated per cycle.
questions.explain: Curve Y has the three signs of heavier damping: a lower maximum amplitude, a wider peak, and a peak at a slightly lower frequency. Away from resonance the curves coincide, which is also expected, because damping matters most near resonance, where the amplitude is limited by the energy dissipated per cycle.

figure.alt: Graph of amplitude (vertical axis, no scale) against driving frequency / Hz (horizontal axis marked 0, 2, 4, 6, 8) with two curves. Curve X, blue, has a tall narrow peak at 4 Hz and falls steeply to small amplitudes on either side. Curve Y, red, has a peak about one third as high as X's, much broader, and centred slightly below 4 Hz. At frequencies well below the peaks (under about 2 Hz) and well above them (over about 6 Hz) the two curves almost coincide.

questions.q: A radar speed detector at the roadside emits microwaves of frequency f along a straight road. The microwaves reflected from a car on the road are detected with a frequency slightly lower than f. What can be deduced about the car?
options: It is a long way from the detector, whatever its motion.
It is at rest, and the microwaves lost energy on reflection.
It is moving along the road, away from the detector.
Nothing about its motion: no Doppler shift occurs at road speeds.
optionWhy: A student who links the Doppler shift to distance expects a distant car to return a lower frequency. Distance affects only the strength of the reflected signal; the frequency shift depends on the car's velocity along the beam.

A student who links frequency to energy expects the weaker reflected wave to have a lower frequency. Reflection from a car at rest reduces the amplitude but leaves the frequency unchanged; a lower frequency shows that the car is moving away.

A lower frequency means the reflected wavefronts return less often than they were emitted, which happens when the reflector is receding. Radar speed detectors use the size of this shift to find the car's speed.

A student who thinks electromagnetic waves are too fast to show a Doppler effect at everyday speeds concludes that the small change is not caused by the car. The fractional shift is tiny, of the order of v/c, but it is measurable, and it is exactly what radar speed detectors use.
questions.explain: A lower frequency means the reflected wavefronts return less often than they were emitted, which happens when the reflector is receding. Radar speed detectors use the size of this shift to find the car's speed.

questions.q: A wavefront diagram shows the sound from a stationary source in still air as circular wavefronts centred on the source. An observer walks directly towards the source at constant speed. Which statement about the waves and the observer is correct?
options: The wavelength is unchanged, but the observer meets the wavefronts more often.
The observer's motion squeezes the wavefronts, so the wavelength is shorter.
The observer detects the emitted frequency, as the source sets it.
The frequency detected rises steadily as the observer nears the source.
optionWhy: The source is at rest, so the wavefronts stay concentric and one emitted wavelength apart; the observer cannot change the wave in the air. Walking towards the source, the observer meets the wavefronts at the relative speed v + u_o instead of v, so more wavefronts are met each second and the frequency detected is higher.

A student who carries the moving-source picture over to the observer expects the wavefronts to crowd together. The observer's motion does not alter the waves in the air: the wavelength stays the same and only the rate at which wavefronts are met changes.

A student who thinks frequency is fixed by the source expects no change. The frequency detected is the number of wavefronts met each second, and an observer walking towards the source meets them more often, so the detected frequency is higher.

A student who links the shift to distance expects the frequency to keep rising as the observer gets closer. The rate of meeting wavefronts depends on the observer's speed, which is constant, so the detected frequency is raised by a constant amount.
questions.explain: The source is at rest, so the wavefronts stay concentric and one emitted wavelength apart; the observer cannot change the wave in the air. Walking towards the source, the observer meets the wavefronts at the relative speed v + u_o instead of v, so more wavefronts are met each second and the frequency detected is higher.

questions.q: Over a cycle lasting 12 days, the absorption lines in the spectrum of a star shift to slightly longer wavelengths, return to their laboratory values, shift to slightly shorter wavelengths, return to their laboratory values, and then repeat the cycle. What can be deduced from these observations?
options: The star's distance varies; its lines are longest when it is farthest.
The star's temperature varies, so its light is alternately redder and bluer.
The speed of the star's light alternately increases and decreases.
The star's velocity along our line of sight alternates in direction.
optionWhy: A student who links the shift to distance expects the longest wavelengths at the greatest distance. The shift depends on velocity: when an orbiting star is farthest away it is momentarily moving across our line of sight, and its lines are at their laboratory values.

A student who takes 'redshift' to mean the light becomes redder explains the change by temperature. A change of temperature alters the colour of the continuous spectrum; it does not move every absorption line by the same fraction. Periodic line shifts show periodic motion.

A student who thinks light from a moving source travels at c plus or minus the source's speed explains the shift by a change in the light's speed. Light from any source travels at c; the source's motion changes the observed wavelength and frequency, not the speed.

A redshift shows the star moving away from us and a blueshift shows it moving towards us. A regular alternation between the two, passing through zero shift, shows the star moving to and fro along our line of sight; the usual cause is orbital motion about a companion star or planet, and the size of the shift gives the speed along the line of sight.
questions.explain: A redshift shows the star moving away from us and a blueshift shows it moving towards us. A regular alternation between the two, passing through zero shift, shows the star moving to and fro along our line of sight; the usual cause is orbital motion about a companion star or planet, and the size of the shift gives the speed along the line of sight.
